newsitem.title: USA: U.S. oil industry sees "stealth" attack underway.
newsitem.headline: U.S. oil industry sees "stealth" attack underway.

text.p: The U.S. oil industry voiced fears Monday that new government agencies, unaccountable to no one, were out to get them and ruin the economy.

New government-based entities, domestic and international, have been formed to come up with environmental policies which could hurt businesses, especially the oil industry, said American Petroleum Institute (API) president Charles DiBona.

These new groups, such as the 37-state Ozone Transport Assessment Group and the International Panel on Global Climate Change, are "removed from the checks of democratic elections and insulated from control by legislative bodies," he said.
"As a result, destructive policies can sneak through the nation's political defenses, wreaking economic havoc before we know what hit us," DiBona said at the API's annual meeting.

Both the Ozone Transport Assessment Group (OTAG) and the global climate change panel are due to issue recommendations next year which could result in heavy taxes on fossil fuels or new curbs on cars and manufacturers.
Exxon chairman Lee Raymond, who is the chairman of API, said any move to combat global climate change by reducing fossil fuel use would be premature.

"There's simply no reason to take drastic action now. But drastic action is exactly what the United States has proposed," he said, referring to the Clinton administration's support for the international effort to set binding limits on carbon dioxide emissions beyond the year 2000.

DiBona said groups like OTAG ignore economics in devising their policies. "Most government stealth groups are dedicated to the pursuit of some single value, so they have little interest in cost-effectiveness or even in costs," he said.
He rejected the view that the new groups, created by government agencies, did not have any power themselves and could only make recommendations.
"Government by stealth puts new demands on all of us. We must invent new ways to confront this mischief," he said.
